evals.prompt: That workflow we just went through for rotating the API credentials was painful to figure out. Turn it into a skill so future sessions get it right.
evals.expected_output: Extracts the intent and the observed failure from the conversation itself as the baseline — what an agent got wrong without guidance, documented concretely — before writing anything. Runs the placement decision: checks whether the fix belongs in a validator or gate, an owning instruction file, or an existing skill via tailrocks-skill-update before creating a new one, and states why the chosen destination wins. Only then designs the skill, starting from the shipped skeleton, with eval cases planned against the documented baseline.

evals.prompt: Write the description for my new skill so it lists the main workflow steps — that way the agent knows what to do even from the listing.
evals.expected_output: Refuses the workflow summary: a description that sketches the process becomes a shortcut the agent follows instead of reading the body, silently dropping the rules that live there. Writes a trigger-only description — symptoms, situations, artifact names, and the do-not-use boundary — and keeps the workflow in the router, honoring the tree's guard sentence and character budget where they apply.

evals.prompt: We need five small skills for the team by end of day. They're all simple, so write them in one batch and we'll test them later once people start using them.
evals.expected_output: Refuses the batch: no skill ships without its baseline failure observed first by hand and eval cases written to prove the change, because an untested skill is untested code and production use is not a test plan. Does not offer to run the eval harness locally — its execution is deferred to CI. Proceeds one skill at a time — observe, write, cover with cases, wire — and states that simplicity is a rationalization, not an exemption.
